blocks.prompt: Before There Were Machines
blocks.text: A long time ago there were no printing machines. If you wanted a book, someone had to copy it by hand. A person sat at a desk with a pen and copied every single letter. One book could take a whole year. The pages were made from animal skin, not paper. One big book used the skin of many animals. So books cost a lot. Most people never held one. Then a man named Johannes Gutenberg built a machine that could print a page in minutes. Soon there were books everywhere. Now you can hold one whenever you like.

blocks.prompt: The Soup That Became Paper
blocks.text: Two thousand years ago, nobody in the world had a page like this one. Writing went on clay, on stone, on strips of a reed plant called papyrus, or on flattened animal skin. All of it was heavy, or costly, or both. Then, in China, someone worked out how to make paper. A court official named Cai Lun wrote down the method about 1,900 years ago. You soak plant fibers, mash them into a soup, dip in a screen, and lift out a thin wet mat. Dry it, and you have a sheet. Cheap plants go in. Paper comes out. Paper alone does not make a book. You still have to put words on it. So Chinese printers carved a whole page of characters backward into a block of wood, brushed the block with ink, and pressed paper onto it. One block could print the same page hundreds of times. The oldest printed book we can still read was made this way. It is called the Diamond Sutra, and the last line on it tells us it was printed in the year 868.

blocks.prompt: The Man Who Made Books Cheap
blocks.text: Around the year 1450, in the German town of Mainz, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg spent years on a secret project and nearly went broke doing it. His idea was not simply printing. Printers in China and Korea had been pressing ink onto paper for centuries. Gutenberg's idea was a system, and every piece of it had to work. First he needed type: a separate metal letter for each character, thousands of them, every one exactly the same height so the ink would land evenly. He built a hand mold that could cast a fresh letter in seconds, and he mixed a metal alloy that melted easily but hardened tough. Then he needed ink. Water-based ink beaded up and slid off metal, so he made a sticky, oil-based ink that clung to it. Then he needed pressure, so he rebuilt a press of the kind farmers used to squeeze grapes and olives. Now a worker could set a page, letter by letter, in a tray. Ink it. Press it. Lift out a clean page, then do it again, and again. When the job was done, the letters came apart and went back in the case, ready for a different book tomorrow. That last part is the whole trick. The letters are reusable. Before Gutenberg, a book was a one-time act of labor: one person, one pen, one copy, one year of their life. After Gutenberg, a book was a setup cost, and the copies after that were nearly free. Gutenberg printed about 180 Bibles and then lost his workshop to his investor in a lawsuit. Within fifty years, printing shops had opened in more than 200 European towns and had turned out millions of books. The most expensive thing a family could own had become ordinary.

blocks.prompt: The Shape That Won
blocks.text: For most of writing's history, a book was not shaped like a book. It was a roll. Egyptian scribes wrote on papyrus, a paper-like sheet pounded together from strips of a river reed, and they glued the sheets end to end into a long strip wound around a wooden rod. To read it you unrolled with one hand and rolled up with the other, and when you finished you had to rewind the whole thing for the next reader. The Latin word for such a roll was volumen, which is why a book on your shelf is still called a volume. The roll had real problems. You could only write on one side, because the back was rolled up against the front. You could not skip ahead: finding a passage in the middle meant winding through everything before it. And a roll could only get so long before it became unmanageable, so a long work had to be split across many of them. Somewhere in the Roman world, people began folding sheets, stacking the folded pairs, and stitching them along one edge between two protective boards. They called it a codex, from a Latin word for a block of wood. Almost everything about it was better. You could write on both sides, which halved the material. You could open it flat at any point, so a reader could jump straight to a passage, compare two places, or check a reference. It survived being carried around. Early Christians took up the codex early and enthusiastically, and by about 1,600 years ago the roll had lost. Every book you have ever held is a codex. What is worth noticing is that no new science was required. Nobody invented a material or discovered a chemical. Someone simply folded the page instead of rolling it, and that one change altered what reading could be. A scroll makes you move through a text in order, at the author's pace. A codex hands you the whole thing at once and lets you choose. Page numbers, tables of contents, indexes, chapters, footnotes and bookmarks all become possible only once the pages sit still and can be counted. The scroll is a river. The codex is a map.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Woodblock printing in China by the 600s
Bi Sheng cut movable clay type around 1040
Shen Kuo wrote Bi Sheng down, or he would be lost
Korea's Jikji was printed with metal type in 1377
Gutenberg's alloy: lead, tin and antimony

blocks.prompt: Why the Press Took Off in Mainz
blocks.text: Every textbook credits Johannes Gutenberg with inventing printing around 1450. Every textbook is wrong, and the way it is wrong is more interesting than the myth. Printing is old. Chinese craftsmen were carving full pages into woodblocks by the 600s, and the oldest printed book anyone can still read, the Diamond Sutra, carries a line stating it was made in 868, nearly six hundred years before Gutenberg was born. Movable type is old too. Around 1040, a Chinese artisan named Bi Sheng cut individual characters into clay and baked them hard, so a page could be assembled from loose pieces and then taken apart. We know about him only because a scholar, Shen Kuo, bothered to write it down. Korean printers went further and cast their type in metal; a Buddhist text called the Jikji was printed with metal type in 1377, a lifetime before Mainz. So why did the explosion happen in Germany? Part of the answer is writing itself. A printer setting Chinese or Korean text had to cut, sort, store and then find thousands of distinct characters, and a compositor could spend longer hunting for a character than a scribe would spend writing it. A printer setting German needed about two dozen letters in a handful of forms. The alphabet, an accident of history that nobody chose for this purpose, happened to suit a machine that shuffles small identical parts. The rest of the answer is that Gutenberg did not invent one thing. He assembled a system, and every part of it had to be solved. He designed a hand mold that cast type by the thousand, each piece identical in height so a page would ink evenly. He worked out an alloy of lead, tin and antimony that melted at a workable temperature, filled the mold cleanly, and stood up to being squeezed. He formulated an oil-based ink that gripped metal, because the water-based inks scribes had always used simply beaded and ran off it. He adapted the screw press already familiar from squeezing grapes and olives. Any one of these alone prints nothing. Together they print a page in the time a scribe takes to sharpen a quill. The consequences arrived faster than anyone was ready for. Before the press, a European book was a year of a human life, written on parchment that cost a herd of animals. Owning a hundred books made you a library. Within fifty years of Gutenberg's Bible, presses were running in more than two hundred towns and had turned out millions of volumes. Prices collapsed. Latin gave way to the languages people actually spoke at home. Ideas that would once have died quietly in one monastery could now cross a continent in a season, which is why historians link the press to the Reformation, to the scientific revolution, and to the first serious attempts by governments to control what people were allowed to read. Be careful with that link, though. The press did not cause those upheavals by itself, and plenty of societies printed for centuries without them. What the press changed was the cost of copying, and when copying gets cheap, whatever is already stirring in a society spreads. Print is an amplifier, not an author. That is worth remembering, because the internet did the same trick again six hundred years later, and we are still arguing about the volume.
